fragments.text: What this project is really about

The goal is not to maximize model complexity. The goal is to turn an ambiguous human need into a reliable computational process: understand → decompose → represent → decide → execute → verify → improve.
A modern computing project framed around judgment, system design, and evidence — not just code generation.

In academic and professional environments, users rarely express problems as clean specifications. They ask vague questions, provide incomplete constraints, mix factual lookup with planning, and expect the system to know when it should search, calculate, ask for clarification, or refuse. A Smart Virtual Assistant is therefore an ideal Computational Thinking project: the technical challenge is not merely generating text, but designing the computational process behind the response.

fragments.text: AI is one computational component, not the architecture. Use AI where uncertainty, language, perception, or synthesis justifies it. Use deterministic logic where correctness, constraints, or repeatability matter more.
These requirements define the expected engineering depth; teams may go beyond them when justified.
A specific target user, pain point, 8–12 representative use cases, explicit non-goals, constraints, and measurable success criteria.
At least one rule/algorithm/calculation/workflow that is transparent and testable.
At least one structured or unstructured information source with documented provenance, metadata, and retrieval logic.
At least one AI/ML/LLM capability whose use is technically justified by the problem.
An explicit mechanism that decides which capability should handle a request; include clarification and fallback paths.
A user-facing interface or demonstrable API flow connected to the real backend/system logic.
Input validation, error handling, timeout/failure behavior, privacy rules, and relevant misuse or prompt-injection defenses.
A repeatable benchmark/test set, metrics or evaluation rubric, error taxonomy, and evidence of at least one improvement cycle.
Choose a domain because it creates an interesting computational problem — not because it sounds fashionable.
Turn deadlines, progress, learning resources, and available time into an adaptive study plan.
Core ideas: Scheduling • ranking • retrieval • learner modeling
Convert unstructured requests into tasks, priorities, constraints, and executable schedules.
Core ideas: Task decomposition • priority queues • constraint solving
Search, compare, and synthesize PDFs, notes, reports, and structured records with traceable evidence.
Core ideas: Parsing • indexing • retrieval • RAG • provenance
Extract decisions, action items, owners, deadlines, and unresolved issues across meetings.
Core ideas: Information extraction • temporal reasoning • state tracking
Combine course, campus, regulation, and schedule information into a student-facing assistant.
Core ideas: Search • structured data • planning • routing
Support requirement breakdown, code/document retrieval, test generation, debugging, and change summaries.
Core ideas: Dependency analysis • program context • testing • retrieval
A reference, not a mandatory stack. Your architecture should be simpler when the problem allows it.
Chat or form UI • CLI • mobile/web prototype
Routing • state • policy • tool selection • fallback

Treat the submission as an engineering handoff: another team should be able to understand, run, test, and critique your system.

12–18 pages recommended, excluding appendices. Problem framing, CT reasoning, architecture, data/knowledge design, algorithms/routing, AI role, implementation, risks, evaluation, errors, limitations, roadmap.
Source code, environment/dependency files, sample configuration, reproducible setup/run instructions, and a working demo. Never submit real credentials.
System-context diagram, component diagram, sequence/data-flow diagram, key schemas/data models, pseudocode, and important interface contracts.
Benchmark/test set, expected outputs/labels where applicable, evaluation script or rubric, metrics, error taxonomy, regression tests, before/after evidence.
Failure catalogue, threat/privacy analysis, red-team cases, safeguards, fallback/escalation paths, and unresolved risks.
Concise technical story: problem → key decisions → architecture → evidence → demo → limitations → lessons learned.
Weekly task allocation, issues/PRs, meeting/progress notes, contribution summary, and a short record of how AI tools were used and verified.
The rubric rewards evidence of thinking, system quality, and disciplined iteration — not code volume or model size.
Clear user/problem boundary; measurable success; strong decomposition, abstraction, and explicit trade-offs.
Coherent components, interfaces, data/control flow, routing, fallback, and failure-aware design.
Appropriate sources, metadata, provenance, retrieval logic, and traceability.
Well-justified choice of deterministic logic, search, AI, tools, and APIs; avoids unnecessary complexity.
End-to-end system works reliably; components are actually integrated; code/repository is understandable and reproducible.
Failure model, privacy/safety thinking, safeguards, red-team cases, and appropriate abstention/escalation.
Balanced benchmark, meaningful metrics/rubric, error analysis, regression testing, and before/after improvement.
Professional technical communication, evidence-centered demo, clear ownership, and ability to defend decisions.

Final quality matters, but weekly milestone evidence also matters. A polished Week-8 demo cannot fully compensate for weak problem framing, undocumented decisions, fabricated evaluation, or an inability to explain how the system works.
Use modern AI tools as engineering aids, while preserving understanding, accountability, and reproducibility.
• Team size: 5–7 students unless approved otherwise.
• Maintain a shared Git repository, issue/task board, and weekly project log.
• Every member should contribute across analysis, design, implementation, evaluation, and communication—not only one isolated role.
• Important design changes should be documented briefly (for example in README notes, issues, or lightweight ADR-style records).
• ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Copilot, and similar tools may be used for brainstorming, code assistance, debugging, writing support, or test generation.
• The team remains responsible for understanding, adapting, verifying, and testing all generated content or code.
• AI-generated text/code is not evidence by itself. Technical claims and evaluation results must come from the team’s sources, code, measurements, or experiments.
• Do not upload secrets, private credentials, restricted data, or sensitive university/company information to public repositories or external AI services.
